title: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Reference-free metrics such as faithfulness, answer relevance, and context relevance enable automated assessment of RAG pipelines when ground-truth annotations are unavailable. | LLM-based decomposition into atomic statements and verification against retrieved context can diagnose grounding failures and unreliable evidence use in RAG systems. | Dedicated evaluation toolkits (RAGAs) and datasets (WikiEval) provide standardized infrastructure for measuring how robustly RAG systems handle context relevance and faithfulness.
rationale: RAGAs introduces a widely adopted reference-free evaluation framework with three core metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance, context relevance) directly targeting whether RAG outputs are grounded in retrieved evidence and whether retrieved context is focused — both central concerns for robust RAG under unreliable evidence. It also releases the WikiEval dataset and an open-source library integrated with LangChain/LlamaIndex, making it a backbone reference in the RAG evaluation literature. It fits the main evaluation section of the survey as a standard tool, though its reliance on a single proprietary LLM (gpt-3.5-turbo-16k) and small-scale human alignment (50 Wikipedia pages) should be noted as a limitation. Overclaim risk is low if presented as an evaluator with known LLM-judge biases rather than a ground-truth oracle.
caveat: Metrics depend on a closed LLM judge and were validated on a small (50-page) WikiEval set, so reported human-agreement numbers may not transfer to harder evidence-conflict or adversarial settings.
notes: EACL 2024 System Demonstrations; code at github.com/explodinggradients/ragas, dataset at huggingface.co/datasets/explodinggradients/WikiEval.

title: BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models
supports_claims: BEIR provides a heterogeneous zero-shot retrieval benchmark spanning 18 datasets and 9 tasks, exposing that in-domain retrieval performance does not predict out-of-distribution generalization—a core concern for RAG retrievers facing unreliable or domain-shifted evidence. | Analysis of annotation selection bias (e.g., lexical bias in TREC-COVID) demonstrates that retrieval evaluation itself can be unreliable, motivating careful evaluation protocols for evidence quality in RAG. | BM25 remains a strong zero-shot baseline while dense retrievers can underperform on shifted domains, informing retriever choice and robustness considerations in RAG pipelines.
rationale: BEIR is a foundational NeurIPS 2021 benchmark that systematically evaluates retrieval models' zero-shot generalization across diverse tasks and domains, making it a backbone reference for any survey discussing evaluation of retrieval components in RAG. Its findings on OOD generalization gaps and lexical annotation bias directly support survey claims about unreliable evidence sources and the limits of in-domain retriever evaluation. It is appropriately placed in main:evaluation as a key benchmark citation for the evaluation perspective. Overclaim risk is low if framed as a retriever-evaluation benchmark rather than an end-to-end RAG evaluation.
caveat: BEIR evaluates retrievers in isolation rather than end-to-end RAG with generators, and is English-only with limited long-document and multi-field coverage; survey should not present it as a full RAG benchmark.
notes: Widely cited foundational retrieval evaluation benchmark; code and data publicly available at UKPLab/beir.

title: DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Real-time Information Needs of Large Language Models
supports_claims: Dynamic/adaptive RAG can decide when to retrieve based on token-level uncertainty, attention importance, and semantic content rather than fixed rules. | Query formulation that leverages self-attention over the full generated context can better capture the model's real-time information needs than using only the last sentence or last few tokens. | Unnecessary retrieval can introduce noisy evidence and harm generation quality, motivating selective/adaptive retrieval triggers.
rationale: DRAGIN is an ACL 2024 long paper that proposes a dynamic RAG framework with two well-defined modules: RIND for retrieval timing (combining entropy, max self-attention, and stopword filtering) and QFS for query formulation from self-attention over the full context. It explicitly frames unnecessary or poorly-timed retrieval as a source of noisy/unreliable evidence, making it a natural citation for the action-control axis of robust RAG (when/what to retrieve, adaptive triggering). It compares against FLARE, IRCoT, IC-RALM, and RETRO baselines on 4 knowledge-intensive datasets with 3 LLMs, providing useful empirical grounding for adaptive-retrieval claims.
caveat: The method requires access to internal self-attention scores, limiting applicability to API-only LLMs; evaluation is limited to knowledge-intensive QA and does not test under adversarial or corrupted-corpus conditions.
notes: Code/data available at https://github.com/oneal2000/DRAGIN; strong fit for an 'adaptive retrieval / when-and-what to retrieve' subsection in the action-control chapter.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
supports_claims: RAG is defined as combining parametric seq2seq generation with non-parametric retrieval over a dense Wikipedia index, providing the canonical formulation for retrieval-augmented generation. | Non-parametric memory in RAG is updatable (index hot-swapping) and reduces hallucinations relative to parametric-only baselines, motivating reliability concerns the survey addresses.
rationale: This is the seminal NeurIPS 2020 paper introducing RAG (RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token) by coupling DPR with BART for knowledge-intensive tasks. Any survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence must cite it as the foundational formulation and as motivation for grounding, factuality, and updateable memory. It also provides early evidence on hallucination reduction and the value of retrieval, which frame later work on evidence reliability. Overclaim risk is low so long as it is cited as foundation rather than as a robustness/security contribution.
caveat: The paper does not directly address unreliable/noisy evidence, attacks, or calibration; cite as foundational rather than as evidence for robustness mechanisms.
notes: Canonical RAG reference; HuggingFace implementation available.

title: LongRAG: A Dual-Perspective Retrieval-Augmented Generation Paradigm for Long-Context Question Answering
supports_claims: Long-context RAG suffers from chunking-induced loss of global structure and low evidence density, motivating extractor-plus-filter pipelines. | CoT-guided filtering combined with mapping chunks back to source paragraphs can reduce noise and improve robustness over Self-RAG and CRAG on multi-hop QA.
rationale: LongRAG proposes a dual-perspective RAG paradigm with an LLM-augmented information extractor and a CoT-guided filter to handle low evidence density and noisy retrievals in long contexts. It directly contributes to robust RAG under unreliable evidence by filtering irrelevant chunks while preserving global context, and compares against Self-RAG/CRAG on multi-hop benchmarks. Placement in main:modality fits because its core insight is scenario-specific (long-context multi-hop QA) while also informing evidence-construction strategies. Overclaim risk is moderate since gains depend on one-time retrieval quality and on fine-tuning data generated by an LLM teacher.
caveat: Authors note dependence on one-time retrieval quality and potential annotation bias from LLM-generated fine-tuning data; gains are reported on three multi-hop datasets only.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main conference; code at https://github.com/QingFei1/LongRAG.

title: RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
supports_claims: Adaptive retrieval methods that decide when to invoke retrieval require careful evaluation, and vanilla prompting is insufficient for guiding LLMs to make reliable retrieval decisions. | Benchmarks targeting knowledge absent from LLMs can isolate the evaluation of retrieval necessity decisions in adaptive RAG. | In-context demonstrations with time awareness can improve adaptive retrieval without calibration or additional training.
rationale: This ACL Findings 2024 paper introduces RetrievalQA, a benchmark of 1,271 short-form QA items whose answers are not in LLM parametric knowledge, enabling clean evaluation of adaptive retrieval decisions. It systematically compares calibration-based (e.g., Self-RAG threshold tuning) and model-based (vanilla prompting) ARAG approaches and proposes TA-ARE, a simple ICL-based method. The work is directly relevant to the action-control axis of robust RAG (when to retrieve, abstention, adaptive routing) and also contributes evaluation insight, making main_cite under main:control appropriate.
caveat: Scope is limited to short-form open-domain QA; does not assess long-form generation, retrieval quality, or noisy-context robustness directly.
notes: Useful as both an adaptive-retrieval method reference and a benchmark for ARAG evaluation.

title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
supports_claims: LLMs exhibit a U-shaped position bias when using retrieved evidence, performing worst when relevant information appears in the middle of long input contexts. | Reader performance saturates well before retriever recall in open-domain QA, indicating that adding more retrieved documents yields diminishing returns and motivates reranking or truncation for robust RAG. | Extended-context models are not necessarily better at using their input context, complicating naive scaling solutions for evidence-rich RAG pipelines.
rationale: This TACL paper provides controlled empirical evidence that LLMs fail to robustly use retrieved evidence depending on its position in the context, with a characteristic U-shaped accuracy curve in multi-document QA and key-value retrieval. It directly informs robust RAG by showing that even when correct evidence is supplied, models may fail to ground on middle-positioned passages, and that more retrieved documents do not guarantee better answers. It is a foundational reference for the model-evidence-use perspective and motivates reranking, context compression, and adaptive retrieval research. Risk of overclaiming is low since findings are specific to evaluated models and prompt formats.
caveat: Findings are tied to specific 2023-era models and prompt formats; later models with improved long-context training may exhibit mitigated but not eliminated positional bias.
notes: Highly influential paper that should anchor any discussion of how LLMs use retrieved evidence under varying context positions and lengths.

title: Model Internals-based Answer Attribution for Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Model internals (gradient-based saliency over context tokens) can produce more faithful answer attributions in RAG than self-citation prompting or external NLI validators. | Self-citation and NLI-based attribution are brittle under instruction-following failures and surface lexical overlap, motivating internals-based faithfulness checks for trustworthy RAG.
rationale: The paper introduces MIRAGE, a two-step internals-based attribution method that detects context-sensitive tokens and traces them to retrieved documents via contrastive feature attribution, then evaluates against self-citation and NLI baselines on XOR-AttriQA and ELI5. It directly addresses faithfulness and grounding of model answers to retrieved evidence—central to robust RAG under unreliable evidence—and documents concrete failure modes of self-citation (missing/wrong citations) and NLI (surface-overlap false positives). It fits the model_evidence_use perspective as a main citation supporting the survey's discussion of attribution/faithfulness mechanisms.
caveat: Evaluated only on 7B open-source LLMs and uses NLI (TRUE) as a proxy reference on ELI5, which the authors acknowledge as a brittleness limitation; generalization to larger models and broader domains is not demonstrated.

title: The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
supports_claims: RAG systems are vulnerable to prompt-based extraction attacks that leak private retrieval database contents. | Integrating retrieval data can paradoxically reduce LLM training-data memorization leakage, while introducing new retrieval-side privacy risks. | Mitigations such as reranking, summarization, and distance thresholds offer partial defenses with privacy-utility tradeoffs.
rationale: The paper empirically demonstrates a novel composite structured prompting attack that extracts private data from RAG retrieval databases on medical dialogue and email datasets, and shows that RAG integration reduces extraction of LLM training data. It is directly relevant to a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence because retrieval data leakage and adversarial prompt extraction represent core security/integrity threats to RAG trustworthiness. Placement in the security section is appropriate as it formalizes a black-box threat model and evaluates several mitigation strategies. Overclaim risk is moderate since findings are tied to specific LLMs and embedding models tested.
caveat: Results are limited to two datasets and a few LLM/embedding combinations; defense evaluations are preliminary and may not generalize.
notes: Strong fit for security/integrity section of a robust RAG survey.

title: Active Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Active retrieval that triggers based on generation-time confidence (low token probability) outperforms fixed-interval or single-shot retrieval in long-form generation. | Forward-looking queries formed from the anticipated next sentence are more effective than past-context queries for adaptive RAG. | Masking low-confidence tokens or generating targeted sub-questions mitigates error propagation when using model-generated content as retrieval queries.
rationale: FLARE is a canonical work on adaptive/active retrieval that decides when and what to retrieve using token-level confidence and forward-looking sentence generation. It directly contributes to the action-control axis of robust RAG (uncertainty-driven retrieval, routing, regeneration) and is consistently cited as a baseline/lineage method in adaptive RAG research. The paper also discusses query-formulation strategies (masking, question generation) that mitigate distractor risk from unreliable LM-generated queries, which ties to evidence reliability. Placement in main:control is appropriate as a backbone reference.
caveat: Calibration assumption (low probability == knowledge gap) may not hold for newer LLMs; the paper does not directly study adversarial or poisoned evidence robustness.

title: ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
supports_claims: Automated RAG evaluation frameworks decompose quality into context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance, using fine-tuned LLM judges over synthetic query-passage-answer triples. | Prediction-powered inference enables tighter confidence intervals on RAG performance using a small human-annotated validation set combined with judge predictions on unlabeled data. | Lightweight fine-tuned judges generalize across in-domain shifts but degrade under drastic shifts (cross-lingual, text-to-code), motivating evaluation-time robustness considerations.
rationale: ARES is a NAACL 2024 paper introducing a widely-adopted automated evaluation framework for RAG systems that explicitly targets context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance using fine-tuned DeBERTa judges trained on synthetically generated data, with PPI providing statistical confidence intervals. This directly underpins evaluation methodology for robust RAG under unreliable evidence, since faithfulness and context-relevance scoring are central diagnostics for detecting when models misuse noisy or irrelevant retrievals. It belongs in the main evaluation section as a backbone reference alongside RAGAS-style frameworks, with the caveat that it does not specifically address adversarial or poisoned contexts.
caveat: ARES targets general English RAG evaluation and does not specifically test adversarial, poisoned, or knowledge-conflict scenarios that are central to unreliable-evidence robustness; judges also degrade under large domain shifts.
notes: Code/data publicly released on GitHub per abstract; venue is NAACL 2024 main long papers.

title: Controlling Risk of Retrieval-augmented Generation: A Counterfactual Prompting Framework
supports_claims: Counterfactual prompting that perturbs retrieval quality and usage can elicit RAG confidence signals for selective abstention. | Risk-aware metrics (risk, carefulness, alignment, coverage) complement EM/F1 for evaluating RAG abstention under noisy evidence. | RAG models suffer overconfidence on noisy retrieved passages, motivating dedicated risk-control mechanisms beyond LLM-only calibration.
rationale: The paper proposes a counterfactual prompting framework that induces a RAG model to reconsider answers under hypothesized poor retrieval quality or improper usage, then keeps or discards outputs based on answer stability. It introduces an RC-RAG benchmark and four risk-aware metrics (risk, carefulness, alignment, coverage) tailored to abstention under unreliable evidence, evaluating on NQ and TriviaQA with Mistral and ChatGPT. This directly supports the action-control axis of the survey (uncertainty, abstention, refusal in RAG) and offers a concrete method and evaluation protocol for unreliable retrieval contexts.
caveat: Limited to factoid QA in a zero-shot setting; the two latent factors are human-defined and fusion is heuristic, so generalization to multi-hop, long-form, or multimodal RAG is unverified.
notes: Code/benchmark at github.com/ict-bigdatalab/RC-RAG.

title: Do You Know What You Are Talking About? Characterizing Query-Knowledge Relevance For Reliable Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Goodness-of-fit hypothesis testing over query-document similarity statistics can detect out-of-knowledge queries and trigger abstention in RAG systems. | Synthetic in-knowledge queries generated from corpus chunks can approximate the true in-knowledge distribution for calibrating rejection thresholds. | Embedding models' retrieval accuracy can be misaligned with their ability to detect out-of-knowledge queries, motivating separate diagnostics.
rationale: The paper proposes a statistical framework using GoF tests on retrieval similarity statistics (MSS, KNN, Energy, Fisher/Simes meta-tests) to identify single out-of-knowledge queries online and detect query distribution shifts offline using a two-sample KS test. It evaluates seven test statistics against outlier-detection baselines and LM-based relevance scoring across eight QA datasets and two biomedical corpora, and proposes using synthetic queries as a proxy when in-knowledge queries are unavailable. This is directly aligned with action control / abstention under unreliable retrieval evidence, a core topic for robust RAG, making it suitable as a main citation in the control chapter.
caveat: Experiments are concentrated in biomedical QA with relatively small subsets (300 samples), and synthetic queries may be overly simple compared to real user queries, which limits the generality of the empirical conclusions.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main conference paper; no explicit code/data URLs were extracted from the PDF text.

title: Synchronous Faithfulness Monitoring for Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Synchronous monitoring of decoding dynamics (likelihood, uncertainty, context influence, semantic alignment) enables accurate sentence-level faithfulness detection in long-form RAG. | Faithfulness-oriented decoding via backtracking and beam search improves the faithfulness-informativeness tradeoff over abstention, reranking, and contrastive decoding. | Lightweight aggregators over complementary signals can generalize across tasks and models for trustworthy RAG.
rationale: The paper proposes SYNCHECK, a fine-grained faithfulness monitor that aggregates multiple decoding-time signals to detect unfaithful sentences in RAG outputs, plus FOD which uses these signals to guide beam search for more faithful generation. This directly addresses how models use retrieved evidence and how to detect and correct unreliable/unfaithful generation, which is central to robust RAG under unreliable evidence. It is appropriate for the main faithfulness/grounding section because it both characterizes failure modes and provides an actionable intervention mechanism. The work is venue-published (EMNLP 2024) with released code and benchmarks.
caveat: The method assumes sentence-level granularity and adds inference latency from extra forward passes; gains depend on a trained aggregator and may vary across larger or differently-tuned RALMs.
notes: Bridges model_evidence_use (faithfulness detection) and action_control (decoding-time intervention); could also be cross-referenced in a control/abstention discussion.

title: Adaptive Contrastive Decoding in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Handling Noisy Contexts
supports_claims: Adaptive contrastive decoding can dynamically balance parametric and retrieved knowledge based on entropy changes to mitigate the influence of noisy contexts in RAG. | Fixed-weight contrastive decoding methods (CAD, MICD) degrade under noisy retrieval, motivating uncertainty-aware adaptive weighting for robust grounding.
rationale: The paper proposes ACD, a decoding-time method that adjusts the contrastive weight between context-conditioned and parametric logits using entropy reduction as a signal of context informativeness, specifically targeting noisy retrieved contexts in open-domain QA. It directly addresses how models use retrieved evidence under unreliable conditions, making it a strong fit for the model_evidence_use section of a robust RAG survey. The empirical contrast against CAD and MICD across LLaMA/Mistral and three QA datasets provides useful evidence of robustness trade-offs between gold and noisy retrieval. Overclaim risk is limited to short-form QA and base (non-aligned) models, as the authors acknowledge.
caveat: Evaluated only on short-form open-domain QA with base LLMs; behavior under instruction-tuned models and long-form generation is untested.
notes: Could secondarily be tagged action_control due to uncertainty-driven adaptive weighting.

title: ``Knowing When You Don't Know'': A Multilingual Relevance Assessment Dataset for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Multilingual benchmarks like NoMIRACL evaluate LLM ability to abstain when retrieved passages are non-relevant, exposing high hallucination rates across 18 languages. | Hallucination rate vs error rate on non-relevant and relevant subsets quantifies the tradeoff between over-abstention and over-answering in RAG. | Most open LLMs struggle to balance grounding and refusal under unreliable evidence, while GPT-4 offers the best tradeoff.
rationale: The paper introduces NoMIRACL, a human-annotated multilingual benchmark that explicitly evaluates LLM robustness to unreliable retrieved evidence by splitting queries into relevant and non-relevant subsets and measuring hallucination and error rates. It directly addresses the survey's core theme of knowing when to abstain under unreliable retrieval and provides diagnostic findings across many LLMs and languages. As a venue-published evaluation artifact with public code/data, it is a strong main-text citation for the evaluation perspective and motivates discussion of abstention/refusal action control.
caveat: Limited to Wikipedia corpora and to binary answer-present/not-present classification rather than full answer-quality evaluation; SFT findings are based on small models.
notes: Useful as a cross-cutting evaluation citation that also connects to action_control (abstention) and modality/scenario (multilingual).

title: BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Standardized benchmarking libraries are needed to fairly compare RAG components across retrievers, rerankers, and LLMs. | Surface-matching metrics like EM/F1 poorly capture answer correctness in zero-shot RAG; LLM-based metrics correlate better with GPT-4 judgments. | Retrieval quality (especially with reranking) materially impacts generation quality, while some QA benchmarks do not benefit from retrieval and may be unsuitable for RAG evaluation.
rationale: BERGEN is an open-source library and large-scale empirical study standardizing RAG evaluation across retrievers, rerankers, LLMs, datasets, and metrics with 500+ experiments. It directly contributes evaluation insights relevant to robust RAG: showing surface metrics fail on verbose generations, demonstrating that retrieval quality strongly affects downstream outcomes, and identifying datasets where retrieval hurts or is noisy (e.g., ELI5, WoW). This makes it a strong main-text citation in the evaluation section of a robust-RAG survey.
caveat: Focused mainly on QA and zero-shot evaluation with Wikipedia-based corpora; does not directly address adversarial poisoning or fine-grained unreliable-evidence robustness.

title: An Information Bottleneck Perspective for Effective Noise Filtering on Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Information bottleneck objectives can train noise filters that simultaneously maximize useful information and minimize irrelevant retrieved content for RAG. | IB-based filtering can produce empty compressions when retrieved passages are irrelevant, supporting abstention-like behavior under unreliable evidence. | IB provides a unified principle for evaluation metrics, SFT data selection, and RL reward design in noise filtering.
rationale: The paper introduces an information bottleneck framework for filtering noisy retrieved passages in RAG, formalizing the trade-off between conciseness and correctness and explicitly handling the case where retrieval is irrelevant. It evaluates on NQ, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA, achieving very high compression rates while improving answer correctness, which is directly germane to robust RAG under unreliable evidence. It is published at ACL 2024 and contributes both a method and a comprehensive evaluation/training principle for evidence construction. Overclaim risk: the empty-compression behavior depends on filter quality and white-box LLM probability estimates, so abstention is not guaranteed.
caveat: Method depends on white-box LLM probability access for the IB metric and operates only at the extractive filtering level; abstention behavior is heuristic via an additional discard flag.

title: SEER: Self-Aligned Evidence Extraction for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Model-based evidence extraction with self-aligned learning can outperform heuristic context filtering by jointly optimizing faithfulness, helpfulness, and conciseness of extracted evidence. | Listwise-aware preference optimization (LPO) over model-sampled evidence candidates improves downstream RAG QA accuracy while substantially reducing input context length. | Evidence extractors fine-tuned via self-alignment show improved robustness to irrelevant/noisy retrieved passages compared to base extractors.
rationale: SEER proposes a model-based evidence extractor trained via self-aligned preference optimization with three expert signals (AlignScore-based faithfulness, log-prob-based helpfulness, semantic conciseness), directly tackling unreliable/distracting retrieved content—a central concern for robust RAG. It contrasts with heuristic context filtering (FILCO) and includes a noise-injection robustness study (Section 4.4) showing the aligned extractor degrades less under increasing noise-to-signal ratios. The methodology fits main_cite under evidence construction because it offers both a concrete mechanism (self-alignment with listwise-aware LPO) and empirical evidence on three QA benchmarks. The overclaim risk is modest: experiments are limited to mid-scale generators (Flan-T5-XL, Llama2-7B), single retriever (DPR/Wikipedia), and one HotpotQA case still shows the aligned extractor degrading faster than base under high noise.
caveat: Limited to mid-scale LLMs and a single dense retriever; the expert design still requires domain choices, and robustness gains do not hold uniformly across all noise levels and datasets.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main conference paper; ACL Anthology bibkey likely 2024.emnlp-main.178.

title: Searching for Best Practices in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Systematic empirical comparison of RAG pipeline modules (query classification, retrieval, reranking, repacking, summarization) yields actionable best practices balancing accuracy and latency. | Fine-tuning generators with a mixture of relevant and randomly-selected documents improves robustness to irrelevant retrieved context while preserving utilization of relevant evidence. | Hybrid sparse-dense retrieval combined with HyDE and reranking (e.g., monoT5) improves evidence quality for downstream generation.
rationale: This EMNLP 2024 paper systematically searches the RAG design space and empirically identifies best practices across the full pipeline, including chunking, hybrid retrieval, HyDE, reranking, repacking, and summarization (Recomp/LongLLMLingua). Crucially for a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence, it studies generator fine-tuning under different context compositions (Dg, Dr, Dgr, Dgg) and finds that mixing relevant and random documents (Mgr) produces a generator that is robust to irrelevant context while still exploiting relevant evidence. The paper also extends to multimodal 'retrieval-as-generation.' It is a strong main-text citation for the evidence-construction pipeline and a useful reference for noise-robust generator training.
caveat: Best-practice recommendations are dataset- and model-specific (Llama2-7B-Chat on selected QA/fact-checking benchmarks); generalization to adversarial poisoning or systematically misleading evidence is not directly evaluated.
notes: Useful as a pipeline-level reference and also for the noise-mixing fine-tuning recipe relevant to robustness.

title: RAG-QA Arena: Evaluating Domain Robustness for Long-form Retrieval Augmented Question Answering
supports_claims: Cross-domain robustness evaluation for RAG-QA requires long-form coherent reference answers that integrate evidence across multiple documents rather than short extractive spans. | LLM-as-judge pairwise evaluation against human-written long-form references can serve as a scalable, reliable benchmark for RAG-QA systems across diverse domains.
rationale: The paper introduces LFRQA, a 26K-query human-annotated long-form RAG-QA dataset across 7 domains, and proposes RAG-QA Arena, an LLM-judge framework that compares model answers to coherent reference answers. It directly addresses evaluation of RAG systems under cross-domain shift, multi-document integration, and conflicting information reconciliation, which are central concerns for robust RAG. Best placed in the evaluation section as a venue-backed long-form, multi-domain RAG benchmark.
caveat: Focuses on answer-quality evaluation and domain robustness rather than directly on adversarial or noisy evidence robustness; LLM-judge bias and cost are acknowledged limitations.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main; useful as a benchmark reference for long-form, multi-domain RAG evaluation.

title: Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach
supports_claims: Self-reflection-based routing between RAG and long-context inference can preserve answer quality while substantially reducing cost. | Systematic failure analysis shows RAG struggles with multi-hop, general, complex, and implicit queries, motivating adaptive control under unreliable retrieved evidence. | Long-context LLMs and RAG produce highly overlapping predictions, supporting hybrid routing strategies for robust generation.
rationale: The paper benchmarks RAG against long-context LLMs across LongBench and InfiniteBench, and proposes Self-Route, which uses LLM self-reflection to decide whether retrieved chunks are sufficient to answer or fall back to full long-context inference. This directly contributes to the action-control thread of robust RAG (adaptive retrieval, abstention/routing based on self-assessed sufficiency) and provides a categorized failure analysis of when RAG yields unreliable evidence. Main-text placement under control is appropriate; an overclaim risk is treating Self-Route as a general calibration mechanism when it relies on LLM self-judged answerability, which may itself be miscalibrated.
caveat: Self-Route assumes LLMs are well-calibrated in judging answerability; results depend on prompt design and may not transfer to adversarial or poisoned evidence settings.
notes: EMNLP 2024 Industry Track paper; GitHub link in text refers to needle-in-a-haystack reference, not authors' own released code.

title: RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Relevance estimators with calibrated confidence can detect when retrieved contexts are unhelpful and trigger abstention or parametric-knowledge fallback in RAG. | Reranking with a learned relevance score, trained via weak supervision from QA likelihood, improves both context selection and answer marginalization under noisy retrieval.
rationale: The paper introduces RE-RAG, which augments RAG with a relevance estimator that outputs both relative relevance and per-context confidence, enabling decoding strategies such as answering 'unanswerable' or falling back on LLM parametric knowledge when retrieved evidence is unreliable. This directly contributes to action-control and evidence-construction aspects of robust RAG under unreliable evidence, and is empirically validated on NQ and TriviaQA across small LMs and LLMs. It is appropriate for the main text on control/abstention mechanisms, with a secondary tie to reranking. Overclaim risk is limited to single-hop QA generalization, as the authors themselves note.
caveat: Evaluated only on single-hop open-domain QA (NQ, TriviaQA); generalization to multi-hop, multimodal, or adversarial poisoning settings is untested.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main conference paper; combines reranking and confidence-driven abstention/parametric fallback.

title: Retrieving, Rethinking and Revising: The Chain-of-Verification Can Improve Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Chain-of-verification with scoring, judgment, and query revision can correct unreliable retrieval evidence via adaptive re-retrieval in RAG. | Joint training of QA and verification with CoT rationales improves generation consistency when references are imperfect.
rationale: The paper proposes CoV-RAG, which integrates a verification module that scores references and answers, judges correctness, and revises the query to trigger re-retrieval when evidence appears unreliable. It also unifies QA and verification during training to mitigate internal generation errors even when external references are correct. This directly contributes to robust RAG under unreliable evidence and adaptive action control (re-retrieval/revision), with ablations on revision position and chain structure that are useful comparison points.
caveat: Training data quality depends on GPT-4 synthesis and verification annotations; verification is effectively single-round in deployment and may not generalize beyond open-domain QA.
notes: Findings of EMNLP 2024; relevant for action-control/adaptive retrieval section alongside Self-RAG and rewrite-retrieve-read baselines.

title: TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Constructing knowledge-grounded reasoning chains from retrieved documents can filter noise and improve multi-hop RAG performance under unreliable evidence. | Finer-grained KG triples plus autoregressive chain construction help identify and integrate dispersed supporting evidence more reliably than raw document concatenation. | Adaptive chain termination and grounding selections in KG options mitigate hallucination and irrelevant context propagation in RAG readers.
rationale: TRACE directly targets the unreliable-evidence problem in RAG by converting retrieved documents into a KG and autoregressively building reasoning chains to isolate supporting triples, reducing the impact of irrelevant retrievals on multi-hop QA. Its grounded option-based triple selection and adaptive termination provide a concrete mechanism for evidence construction and noise filtering, with strong gains over vanilla RAG and IRCoT on HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue. This makes it a fitting main-text citation in the evidence-construction section of a robust RAG survey. Overclaim risk is limited because evaluation depends on existing retrieved candidate sets and Wikipedia-style title-anchored KG generation.
caveat: Evidence-quality gains are measured only via downstream QA; KG/chain quality is not directly evaluated, and the method assumes accessible token logits and Wikipedia-style title-text documents.
notes: EMNLP 2024 Findings; code at https://github.com/jyfang6/trace

title: Unified Active Retrieval for Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Adaptive/active retrieval that decides when to retrieve is essential for robust RAG, since indiscriminate retrieval can inject irrelevant or harmful evidence. | Multifaceted retrieval-timing criteria (intent, knowledge need, time-sensitivity, self-knowledge) outperform single-criterion approaches like FLARE, Self-RAG, and SKR. | Lightweight plug-and-play classifiers over frozen LLM hidden states enable efficient routing decisions with negligible inference overhead.
rationale: The paper proposes UAR, a unified active-retrieval framework with four orthogonal criteria (intent, knowledge, time-sensitivity, self-awareness) operationalized via plug-and-play classifiers and a UAR-Criteria decision tree, and introduces AR-Bench for evaluating retrieval-timing accuracy. This directly supports the survey's action-control axis on adaptive retrieval and routing under unreliable evidence, showing that retrieval can hurt when knowledge is unneeded or already internalized. It is a strong venue-linked backbone reference for the when-to-retrieve subsection and naturally compares to FLARE/Self-RAG/SKR. Risk: the criteria are heuristic and experiments focus on short-form QA with single-step retrieval, so claims about general robustness should be moderated.
caveat: Limited to single-step retrieval and short-form generation; classifiers may not generalize OOD beyond evaluated scenarios.
notes: Strong fit for action-control/adaptive-retrieval section; AR-Bench may also be cited under evaluation.

title: Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Unsupervised training can teach LLMs to act as information refiners that integrate parametric knowledge with retrieved evidence under varied quality conditions. | Training LLMs to handle three retrieval scenarios (complete, incomplete/incorrect, and irrelevant retrieved texts) improves RAG robustness to noisy and misleading evidence. | Information refinement training enhances zero-shot RAG performance across diverse tasks while preserving generalization.
rationale: The paper proposes INFO-RAG, an unsupervised training method that explicitly addresses three scenarios of retrieved evidence quality including incorrect, incomplete, and irrelevant retrievals, which directly aligns with robust RAG under unreliable evidence. It contributes a model-side mechanism for handling noisy/misleading retrieval and demonstrates robustness gains across 11 datasets. This is a strong main_cite for the model_evidence_use perspective, with clear evaluation of scenario-specific behavior. Code availability supports reproducibility.
caveat: Experiments limited to 7B/13B LLaMA-2 models; the scenario taxonomy is synthetic rather than from real-world noisy retrieval, which may overestimate robustness gains.
notes: ACL 2024 long paper; directly addresses robustness to incorrect/incomplete/irrelevant retrieved evidence.

title: G-Retriever: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Textual Graph Understanding and Question Answering
supports_claims: Graph-based RAG can mitigate hallucination by retrieving structured subgraph evidence directly from textual graphs rather than relying on LLM parametric memory. | Subgraph retrieval can be formulated as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization to balance relevance, connectivity, and context-window-aware size control. | RAG over graphs/KGs scales beyond LLM context limits and supports explainability via retrieved subgraph evidence in QA settings.
rationale: G-Retriever introduces a pioneering RAG framework for general textual graphs, formulating subgraph retrieval as a PCST optimization to return connected, query-relevant evidence while fitting LLM context windows. It explicitly demonstrates and quantifies hallucination reduction (e.g., valid node/edge fractions, fully valid graphs) compared to graph prompt tuning, directly speaking to robust RAG under noisy/structured evidence. As a NeurIPS 2024 paper with strong empirical results, code, datasets, and a GraphQA benchmark, it is a backbone reference for the graph/KG modality chapter of a robust RAG survey.
caveat: The retrieval component is static and PCST-based rather than learned; hallucination evaluation on SceneGraphs is based on a relatively small manual sample (100 responses).
notes: Also relevant as evidence_construction (PCST retrieval) and as a hallucination-mitigation case study for graph RAG.

title: Influence Guided Context Selection for Effective Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Context selection based on holistic quality assessment (query-, list-, and generator-aware) can effectively filter noisy/irrelevant retrieved contexts and improve RAG robustness. | Reframing context quality as an inference-time data valuation problem (Contextual Influence value) enables hyperparameter-free selection by retaining only contexts with positive marginal contribution. | A lightweight surrogate model trained with oracle influence supervision plus end-to-end generator feedback can approximate expensive influence computations at inference.
rationale: The paper directly tackles a core robust-RAG problem: noisy/irrelevant retrieved contexts that mislead the generator. It introduces a principled Contextual Influence value that integrates query-, list-, and generator-aware signals, and trains a hierarchical surrogate (CSM) for efficient inference-time filtering, evaluated across 8 knowledge-intensive tasks with two LLM backbones against strong selection/agentic baselines. This is a venue-backbone contribution to the evidence-construction pillar of the survey, justifying main-text discussion in the evidence/context-selection section. Overclaim risk: gains require per-task training of CSM and oracle CI labels, so generalization across tasks/models remains limited (authors acknowledge this).
caveat: CSM currently requires task-specific training with oracle CI value supervision; cross-task generalization and scaling to very large context lists are not fully demonstrated.
notes: NeurIPS 2025 paper with public code (RAG-CSM). Fits naturally alongside RECOMP, Provence, bge-reranker, RankGPT, and information-bottleneck filtering work in an evidence-construction subsection on context selection/compression for robustness against noisy retrieval.

title: RAGTruth: A Hallucination Corpus for Developing Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
supports_claims: RAGTruth provides a large-scale word-level hallucination corpus tailored to RAG, enabling fine-grained evaluation of unsupported or conflicting outputs given retrieved evidence. | Fine-tuning a smaller LLM on RAGTruth yields hallucination detection competitive with GPT-4 prompt-based methods and can be used to suppress hallucinations at inference time. | Benchmarking shows even with retrieved references, leading LLMs produce baseless or conflicting content, motivating dedicated detection and mitigation components in robust RAG pipelines.
rationale: The paper introduces a venue-published, large-scale word-level hallucination corpus specifically for RAG settings across QA, data-to-text, and summarization, with four hallucination types and detailed span annotations. It benchmarks multiple detection methods (prompting, SelfCheckGPT, LMvLM, fine-tuned Llama) and demonstrates that detectors can reduce hallucination rates substantially when used to select among candidate responses. This directly supports an evaluation-focused section on diagnosing unreliable evidence use and model unfaithfulness in RAG, making it a core benchmark resource for the survey.
caveat: Coverage is limited to three English tasks and six specific LLMs from 2023-era models; generalization of the fine-tuned detector to other domains, languages, or newer models is not validated.
notes: Dataset publicly available at https://github.com/ParticleMedia/RAGTruth; useful for both evaluation and faithfulness/grounding discussions.

title: Measuring and Enhancing Trustworthiness of LLMs in RAG through Grounded Attributions and Learning to Refuse
supports_claims: Alignment via DPO with paired positive/negative responses can substantially improve LLMs' ability to refuse unanswerable RAG queries and ground answers in retrieved documents. | Holistic trustworthiness metrics combining grounded refusals, calibrated answer correctness, and citation precision/recall expose how parametric-knowledge reliance inflates standard RAG scores. | Disentangling retriever quality from LLM groundedness is necessary to measure robust behavior under insufficient or irrelevant evidence.
rationale: The paper introduces TRUST-SCORE (a metric jointly capturing grounded refusal, answer-calibrated correctness, and citation groundedness) and TRUST-ALIGN (a DPO-based alignment recipe with a 19K preference dataset targeting five hallucination types including over-responsiveness and excessive refusal). It directly addresses robust RAG under unreliable evidence by penalizing parametric-knowledge leakage and training models to refuse when documents are insufficient. Placement in the action_control/refusal section is appropriate, with secondary relevance to evaluation and model_evidence_use. Overclaim risk is modest: improvements are mostly on three QA datasets and depend on the TRUE NLI labeler for answerability.
caveat: Evaluation centers on ASQA/QAMPARI/ELI5/ExpertQA and relies on a TRUE-based NLI judge for answerability, which may not generalize to multimodal, agentic, or adversarial unreliable-evidence settings.
notes: Code released at github.com/declare-lab/trust-align; strong candidate as a backbone reference for refusal/abstention and trustworthiness evaluation in RAG.

title: PoisonedEye: Knowledge Poisoning Attack on Retrieval-Augmented Generation based Large Vision-Language Models
supports_claims: Vision-language RAG systems are vulnerable to single-sample knowledge poisoning attacks that manipulate target responses by jointly crafting poison images and texts to satisfy retrievability and inducibility. | Class-targeted multimodal poisoning extends attack reach beyond exact-match queries, and standard defenses like noise, cropping, and RoCLIP only partially mitigate such attacks. | Robust RAG must consider multimodal evidence integrity, since perturbations to retrieval embeddings can cause poisoned image-text pairs to dominate top-K retrieval.
rationale: The paper introduces the first knowledge poisoning attack tailored to vision-language RAG, optimizing poison images so a single injected pair achieves high retrieval and poison success across multiple retrievers and LVLMs. It directly addresses unreliable evidence in multimodal RAG by formalizing retrievability/inducibility properties and demonstrating that existing defenses (noise, crop, RoCLIP) provide limited protection. This is a strong fit for a robust RAG survey's security/integrity section, especially for multimodal scenarios. Overclaim risk: only one poison sample is injected and attacks largely assume white-box retriever access for the strongest variants.
caveat: Strongest variants (PoisonedEye-S/C) assume white-box access to the retriever; evaluation focuses on a single multimodal database (OVEN-Wiki) and a narrow target-response style.
notes: ICML 2025 venue-published; first VLRAG poisoning attack, complementary to PoisonedRAG/TrojanRAG/AgentPoison in the multimodal setting.

title: REAR: A Relevance-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Open-Domain Question Answering
supports_claims: Explicit relevance-assessment modules integrated into RAG architectures can mitigate LLM susceptibility to irrelevant or noisy retrieved documents. | Bi-granularity (coarse binary plus fine-grained preference) relevance supervision combined with noise-resistant training improves adaptive use of parametric versus external knowledge. | Relevance-aware generation enables knowledge-consistency verification between parametric and retrieved evidence for more reliable answer selection.
rationale: REAR adds an explicit relevance-assessment module to an LLM-based RAG pipeline and trains it with bi-granularity relevance fusion plus noise-resistant objectives so the model can adaptively rely on internal or external knowledge depending on document reliability. This directly addresses the survey's core question of how LLMs should behave under unreliable retrieved evidence, with quantitative gains on four open-domain QA benchmarks and explicit comparisons to Self-RAG and RobustLM. It is a venue-published EMNLP 2024 paper with code, making it a strong main-text reference in the model-evidence-use lineage. Overclaim risk is moderate: results are limited to open-domain QA and document-level (not sentence/token-level) relevance.
caveat: Evaluation is restricted to open-domain QA at document granularity; generalization to other knowledge-intensive tasks and finer-grained evidence is untested.
notes: ACL Anthology entry 2024.emnlp-main.321; code at github.com/RUCAIBox/REAR.

title: ReDeEP: Detecting Hallucination in Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Mechanistic Interpretability
supports_claims: RAG models can hallucinate even when retrieved evidence is accurate and relevant, due to overreliance on parametric knowledge in later-layer FFNs and insufficient retention of external context by copying attention heads. | Mechanistic interpretability can decouple a model's use of external evidence versus parametric knowledge, providing diagnostic signals for hallucination detection in RAG. | Detection-time interventions that reweight attention heads and FFN contributions can mitigate hallucinations without parameter updates.
rationale: ReDeEP investigates the internal mechanisms behind RAG hallucinations when retrieved evidence is accurate, identifying that Knowledge FFNs over-inject parametric knowledge while Copying Heads fail to retain external context. It proposes detection (ReDeEP) and mitigation (AARF) methods validated on RAGTruth and Dolly (AC) with LLaMA models, directly addressing model faithfulness to evidence under conditions where retrieval is correct but the model still drifts. This is a venue-backbone contribution for the model_evidence_use perspective in a robust-RAG survey, distinguishing RAG hallucination from knowledge conflict and offering both diagnostic and corrective tools.
caveat: Experiments focus on LLaMA-2/3 families and assume accurate retrieved context, so generalization to noisy/adversarial retrieval and larger or non-decoder architectures is not fully demonstrated.
notes: Strong mechanistic interpretability contribution; pairs well with citations on knowledge conflict, hallucination detection (SelfCheckGPT, EigenScore), and RAGTruth benchmark.

title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
supports_claims: Self-reflection tokens enable adaptive retrieval and on-demand grounding decisions, improving robustness when evidence is unnecessary or unreliable. | Critique tokens for relevance and support provide a fine-grained mechanism to filter retrieved passages and enforce faithfulness during decoding. | Controllable inference via weighted reflection-token scoring allows trading off citation precision, fluency, and retrieval frequency at test time.
rationale: Self-RAG trains an LM to emit reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve, assess passage relevance (IsRel), verify support (IsSup), and rate utility (IsUse), then uses segment-level beam search weighted by these scores. This is a canonical mechanism for action control and grounding under potentially irrelevant or unsupportive evidence, directly addressing key axes of robust RAG. Main-text citation in the action-control section is appropriate, with cross-reference to evidence use and faithfulness. Caveat: relies on GPT-4-distilled critic labels and Wikipedia retrieval, so robustness to adversarial or poisoned evidence is not directly evaluated.
caveat: Reflection tokens are distilled from GPT-4 judgments and the method is not directly evaluated against adversarial or poisoned retrieval contexts.
notes: Widely cited ICLR 2024 backbone for adaptive/self-reflective RAG.

title: Reliable Decision‑Making via Calibration‑Oriented Retrieval‑Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Calibration-oriented reranking can align RAG confidence with empirical decision correctness, mitigating overconfidence when retrieved evidence is unreliable. | Training a forecasting function over query-document pairs enables selective retrieval and query reformulation when no candidate passage provides sufficient decision support.
rationale: CalibRAG proposes a forecasting function f(t,q,d) trained with self-consistency soft labels to predict whether a user's decision based on retrieved evidence will be correct, then uses it both to rerank documents and to abstain/reformulate when confidence falls below a threshold. This directly addresses unreliable retrieval (top-1 documents that mislead) and overconfident RAG outputs, which are core concerns of the survey. It belongs in the action-control section because the central contribution is calibration-driven routing and adaptive retrieval rather than retrieval quality per se. The approach is validated on general QA and medical MIRAGE benchmarks against calibration tuning, verbalized confidence, reranking, and Self-RAG baselines.
caveat: Relies on a surrogate LLM user model and GPT-4o-mini grading, so calibration claims depend on these proxies; synthetic supervision generation adds nontrivial overhead.
notes: NeurIPS 2025 venue-linked; strong fit for the action-control/calibration thread of the survey.

title: MMed-RAG: Versatile Multimodal RAG System for Medical Vision Language Models
supports_claims: Multimodal medical RAG systems must handle domain heterogeneity via domain-aware retrievers and adaptively select the number of retrieved contexts to avoid noise-induced hallucinations. | Preference fine-tuning targeting cross-modality alignment and over-reliance on retrieved evidence mitigates two distinct RAG failure modes (copy-reference and retrieval interference) in vision-language models. | Diagnostic metrics such as Copy-Reference rate and Over-Reliance rate provide useful evaluation tools for measuring RAG robustness under unreliable retrieved evidence.
rationale: MMed-RAG is an ICLR 2025 multimodal medical RAG system that explicitly identifies and mitigates two failure modes induced by unreliable retrieved evidence: cross-modality misalignment (model copies retrieved text while ignoring the image) and over-reliance interference (correct answers flipped to wrong by noisy retrieval). It contributes adaptive context selection via similarity-gap thresholding, domain-aware retriever routing, and RAG-based DPO with constructed preference pairs, plus theoretical analysis of weight shifts. These contributions directly support the survey's main claims on robust RAG under unreliable evidence in the multimodal/medical scenario, justifying main_cite placement in the modality section.
caveat: Scope is limited to medical VLMs and the preference-pair construction depends on the base model already producing some correct vs. incorrect responses; generalization beyond medical imaging is not fully validated.
notes: Strong candidate as a venue-backbone reference for multimodal RAG with unreliable evidence and as evaluation reference for CR/OR diagnostics.

title: Generate-then-Ground in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multi-hop Question Answering
supports_claims: Generate-then-ground frameworks can mitigate noise in retrieved documents by alternating LLM answer generation with evidence-based revision. | Batch grounding strategies and instructional grounding distillation help LLMs ignore plausible-looking but irrelevant retrieved content in multi-hop QA.
rationale: The paper proposes GenGround, an alternative to retrieve-then-read that first generates an answer from parametric knowledge then grounds and revises it using retrieved evidence, explicitly targeting noise and irrelevant content in retrieved documents. It also introduces a batch grounding strategy and instructional grounding distillation for smaller models, with experiments on four multi-hop QA benchmarks. This is directly relevant to robust RAG under unreliable evidence and knowledge conflict between parametric and retrieved sources, making it suitable for the model-evidence-use section. Overclaim risk is modest since the approach still depends on LLM judgment of evidence relevance.
caveat: Evaluation is limited to multi-hop QA with Wikipedia corpora and does not explicitly stress-test adversarial or counterfactual noise beyond standard retrieval imperfections.

title: Benchmarking Multimodal Retrieval Augmented Generation with Dynamic VQA Dataset and Self-adaptive Planning Agent
supports_claims: Heuristic multimodal RAG with fixed two-step retrieval fails on dynamic, multi-hop, or multimodal-knowledge questions because of non-adaptive and overloaded retrieval queries. | Self-adaptive planning agents that decompose complex multimodal questions into sub-question chains and dynamically choose retrieval tools (image/text search) improve robustness over rigid mRAG pipelines. | Dyn-VQA provides a benchmark for evaluating mRAG under rapidly changing answers, cross-modal knowledge needs, and >2-hop reasoning.
rationale: The paper introduces Dyn-VQA, a benchmark targeting dynamic/multimodal/multi-hop questions that expose rigidity failures of heuristic mRAG, and proposes OmniSearch, a self-adaptive planning agent that interleaves sub-question decomposition with tool-conditioned retrieval and feedback. This directly supports a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence by giving both a multimodal evaluation lens and an action-control mechanism that re-routes retrieval when evidence is stale, ambiguous, or insufficient. Placement in the modality/scenario chapter is natural, with secondary support for adaptive-retrieval (action control) and evaluation sections. Overclaim risk: results are largely tied to GPT-4V/Qwen-VL backbones and Google-based retrieval tools, so generality of the agent design beyond these tools is not fully established.
caveat: Evaluation depends on commercial search APIs and proprietary MLLM backbones; F1-recall metric and small benchmark size (~1.5K) limit statistical robustness.

title: Think-on-Graph 2.0: Deep and Faithful Large Language Model Reasoning with Knowledge-guided Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Tight-coupling of KG-based and text-based retrieval through iterative graph-guided context retrieval improves multi-hop reasoning faithfulness and reduces hallucination compared to loose-coupling hybrid RAG. | Iterative knowledge-guided retrieval with context-based entity pruning enables deeper evidence gathering for complex knowledge-intensive QA tasks.
rationale: ToG-2 proposes a hybrid KG+text RAG framework that iteratively performs graph search guided by contextual document retrieval, addressing both the incompleteness of KGs and the lack of structured relations in text-only RAG. It directly contributes to the modality/scenario dimension of robust RAG by showing how structured knowledge can guide more faithful context retrieval, with explicit discussion of hallucination mitigation and refusal behavior. Suitable for the main modality section as a representative graph/KG-augmented RAG approach. Overclaim risk is moderate since improvements depend on KG completeness, which the authors themselves analyze in ablations.
caveat: Performance depends on KG completeness and entity linking quality; the framework is training-free but adds significant runtime and API cost overhead compared to vanilla RAG.

title: Understanding Parametric and Contextual Knowledge Reconciliation within Large Language Models
supports_claims: LLMs route contextual and parametric knowledge through distinct sets of attention heads, with competition occurring within knowledge types rather than across them. | Conflicting evidence persists in residual streams without erasure, while aligned multi-source signals accumulate superpositionally to determine output selection. | Entity-aware probing can mechanistically diagnose how RAG models reconcile knowledge conflicts between retrieved context and parametric memory.
rationale: This NeurIPS 2025 paper introduces an entity-aware probing framework to mechanistically trace how LLMs reconcile parametric and contextual knowledge under conflict in RAG. It provides direct evidence for how models internally handle unreliable or conflicting retrieved evidence, identifying specialized attention heads (context vs memory heads) and showing that conflicting knowledge persists rather than being suppressed. The findings are highly pertinent to a robust-RAG survey's model-evidence-use section, supporting claims about grounding, faithfulness, and knowledge conflict mechanics.
caveat: Experiments rely on synthetic counterfactual entity substitution and decoder-only LLaMA/Qwen models; generalization to naturally occurring conflicts and other architectures is untested.
notes: Code/data release pending company approval at submission time.

title: RAG-DDR: Optimizing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Using Differentiable Data Rewards
supports_claims: Differentiable preference-based training (DPO with rollout rewards) can align data preferences across RAG modules and mitigate knowledge conflict between parametric memory and retrieved evidence. | End-to-end optimization of the generation module improves robustness to noisy retrieved documents and reduces overfitting compared to SFT-based RAG training (e.g., RA-DIT).
rationale: RAG-DDR proposes a DPO-based, rollout-reward training scheme that explicitly optimizes the generation and knowledge refinement agents to handle noisy documents and knowledge conflict, with dedicated Has-Answer / Miss-Answer / Internal Knowledge evaluations and a noise-injection robustness experiment. These are direct contributions to robust RAG under unreliable evidence, fitting the model_evidence_use thread on faithfulness/conflict and adjacent to evidence_construction. The ICLR 2025 publication and released code make it a solid main-text reference for the training/alignment lineage in the survey.
caveat: Improvements on knowledge refinement are limited; effectiveness is shown mainly on standard knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks, not on adversarial/poisoned corpora.

title: LaRA: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Long-Context LLMs – No Silver Bullet for LC or RAG Routing
supports_claims: LaRA provides a rigorous benchmark for comparing RAG and long-context LLMs across four task types (location, reasoning, comparison, hallucination detection) and shows no universal winner. | RAG's relative benefit depends on model strength, context length, and task type, with RAG outperforming LC for weaker models and longer contexts, and notably for hallucination detection. | LC LLMs exhibit lost-in-the-middle behavior while RAG is more robust to answer position, motivating routing strategies under unreliable evidence.
rationale: This ICML 2025 paper introduces LaRA, a 2326-case benchmark systematically comparing RAG vs long-context LLMs across novels, papers, and financial statements with four task types including hallucination detection. It directly supports the survey's evaluation chapter by providing empirical evidence on when RAG helps under long-context conditions and revealing that RAG mitigates hallucination and lost-in-the-middle issues. The benchmark addresses prior evaluation flaws (insufficient context length, data leakage, truncation, unreliable metrics), making it a useful diagnostic resource. Risk of overclaim: results are bounded by their RAG configuration (GTE-large, hybrid search, fixed chunking) and QA-style tasks.
caveat: Findings are tied to a specific RAG configuration and QA-only tasks; conclusions about RAG vs LC routing may not generalize to other retrievers, generative tasks, or noisy/adversarial corpora.
notes: Strong fit for evaluation/long-context sections; also relevant to action_control given routing motivation.

title: Provence: efficient and robust context pruning for retrieval-augmented generation
supports_claims: Context pruning via sequence labeling can dynamically remove irrelevant retrieved sentences and improve robustness to noisy evidence in RAG. | Unifying reranking and context pruning into a single cross-encoder yields near-zero-cost evidence filtering that generalizes across QA domains and context lengths.
rationale: Provence is an ICLR 2025 method that directly addresses unreliable/noisy retrieved evidence by training a DeBERTa-based extractive pruner that adaptively selects relevant sentences (from zero to all) and is jointly trained with a reranker. It is evaluated across diverse QA domains (NQ, HotpotQA, TyDiQA, PopQA, BioASQ, SyllabusQA, RGB) with needle-in-haystack and variable-length analyses, providing concrete evidence-construction insights for robust RAG. The method, model, and code are publicly released, supporting reproducibility and lineage discussion in a survey's evidence-construction section.
caveat: Scope limited to English QA with single-passage processing; gains depend on the chosen threshold and silver-label LLM quality, and the unified reranking head adds a small trade-off versus standalone rerankers.
notes: Strong candidate as a backbone reference for context pruning / noise filtering lineage alongside RECOMP, LLMLingua family, FilCo, COMPACT, and DSLR.

title: ReEval: Automatic Hallucination Evaluation for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models via Transferable Adversarial Attacks
supports_claims: Adversarial perturbation of evidence (answer swapping and context enriching) can dynamically evaluate RAG hallucination beyond static QA benchmarks. | Even state-of-the-art LLMs like GPT-4 fail to faithfully use perturbed evidence, and adversarial test cases transfer across LLMs. | Faithfulness-promoting prompts do not consistently mitigate hallucinations when evidence is perturbed or enriched.
rationale: ReEval presents an automatic evaluation framework that perturbs retrieval evidence via answer swapping and context enriching to test whether RAG LLMs faithfully use provided evidence rather than relying on memorization. This directly addresses unreliable evidence robustness, knowledge conflict, and evaluation diagnostics for RAG, with human-verified naturalness of perturbations and cross-model transferability. It belongs in the evaluation section as a venue-backbone reference for dynamic, adversarial RAG evaluation under evidence perturbation.
caveat: Scope is limited to short-answer single-hop QA; perturbations modify either answer span or surrounding context but not both jointly, limiting coverage of complex unreliable-evidence scenarios.

title: Auto-GDA: Automatic Domain Adaptation for Efficient Grounding Verification in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Lightweight NLI-based grounding verifiers can be domain-adapted via synthetic data to detect ungrounded RAG outputs at low latency | Iterative synthetic data generation with weak teacher labels and label-preserving augmentations closes most of the domain gap for grounding verification in RAG
rationale: Auto-GDA introduces an unsupervised domain adaptation framework that produces synthetic NLI training data to fine-tune lightweight grounding verification models for realistic RAG inputs, reaching LLM-level grounding verification quality at ~10% inference cost. This directly supports robust RAG under unreliable evidence by providing a practical mechanism for post-hoc faithfulness/grounding verification that can flag ungrounded generations before they reach end users. It belongs in the model evidence-use section as a method for detecting unfaithful use of retrieved evidence, with possible secondary placement in action_control since verification scores can drive abstention or correction.
caveat: The paper assumes covariate shift only and access to a representative target-domain evidence corpus; it does not directly study adversarial or poisoned evidence, so reliability claims under malicious unreliable evidence should not be overstated.
notes: ICLR 2025 paper with Amazon-science code release; evaluates on RAGTruth, LFQA-Verification, SummEdits.

title: RAGGED: Towards Informed Design of Scalable and Stable RAG Systems
supports_claims: Reader robustness to noisy retrieval, rather than retriever quality alone, is the dominant factor governing RAG stability and scalability across retrieval depths. | Systematic evaluation metrics like RAG Stability Score (RSS) and RAG Scalability Coefficient (RSC) provide principled diagnostics of RAG behavior under realistic, non-oracle retrieval conditions. | Prompting interventions for noise filtering are inconsistent and cannot substitute for reranking or reader noise robustness, particularly in specialized domains.
rationale: RAGGED introduces a systematic framework and two new metrics (RSS, RSC) for evaluating RAG behavior across retrieval depths, retrievers, readers, and datasets under realistic (non-oracle) retrieval. It directly characterizes peak-then-decline vs. improve-then-plateau reader behaviors and shows that reader noise sensitivity is the key determinant of RAG reliability—central concerns for a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence. The evaluation methodology and findings on prompting vs. reranking are directly applicable to the survey's evaluation chapter and the discussion of model-side handling of noisy contexts.
caveat: Evaluation is limited to QA-style benchmarks (NQ, HotpotQA, BioASQ, preliminary CRAG) and does not cover adversarial or poisoned evidence; metrics emphasize aggregate stability rather than per-instance failure modes.
notes: ICML 2025 (PMLR v267); code and data at https://github.com/neulab/ragged. Strong candidate for the evaluation section and as supporting evidence for the model-evidence-use discussion of noise robustness.

title: Simple is Effective: The Roles of Graphs and Large Language Models in Knowledge-Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: KG-based RAG can balance retrieval coverage and LLM context limits by using lightweight MLP triple scoring with directional distance encoding to produce flexible, size-adjustable subgraphs. | Truth-grounded evaluation metrics (scoreh) and refusal behavior when evidence is insufficient improve reliability and reduce hallucinations in RAG pipelines. | Retrieval size must be matched to LLM reasoning capacity since irrelevant retrieved triples can degrade smaller LLMs even while helping larger ones.
rationale: SubgraphRAG introduces an efficient triple-factorized subgraph retriever with DDE for KGQA and demonstrates how flexible subgraph size affects downstream LLM grounding, including refusal-to-answer when evidence is missing. It directly addresses unreliable-evidence concerns by measuring truth-grounded answer behavior (scoreh) and analyzing how different LLM reasoners tolerate irrelevant retrieved triples. It fits the modality/scenario section as a representative KG-RAG backbone with explicit reliability and grounding analysis.
caveat: Evaluation is limited to WebQSP/CWQ over Freebase and does not directly test adversarial poisoning or conflicting evidence; reliability claims rest on hallucination reduction via grounding rather than robustness to corrupted retrieval.
notes: ICLR 2025 paper with public code at Graph-COM/SubgraphRAG; useful as a KG-RAG scenario case with explicit truth-grounding metric and refusal behavior.

title: SePer: Measure Retrieval Utility Through The Lens Of Semantic Perplexity Reduction
supports_claims: Semantic perplexity reduction can quantify retrieval utility as belief shift in the generator, providing finer-grained signal than lexical match or NDCG-style metrics. | Evaluation of RAG should jointly consider retrieval quality and the LLM's prior knowledge, since irrelevant or already-known evidence yields zero utility. | Partial or intermediate evidence in multi-hop RAG can be diagnosed via knowledge-gain metrics rather than end-to-end accuracy alone.
rationale: The paper proposes SePer and Delta-SePer, sampling-based metrics that measure retrieval utility as the LLM's semantic belief shift toward ground-truth answers, and validates them against human judgments across simple and multi-hop QA datasets. For a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence, this provides a principled evaluation lens for diagnosing when retrieved evidence is helpful, redundant, irrelevant, or noisy, including ablations over rerankers, prompt compression, and number of retrieved items. Main:evaluation placement is appropriate because the contribution is methodological for evaluation rather than a robustness mechanism per se. Overclaim risk: the metric requires reference answers and assumes calibrated semantic clustering, so it is not directly a robustness defense.
caveat: Metric requires gold answers and Monte-Carlo sampling; does not itself defend against poisoned or adversarial evidence, only diagnoses utility.
notes: ICLR 2025 published; code at github.com/sepermetric/seper.

title: FaithEval: Can Your Language Model Stay Faithful to Context, Even If "The Moon is Made of Marshmallows"
supports_claims: Contextual faithfulness of LLMs degrades sharply under unanswerable, inconsistent, and counterfactual evidence, even for state-of-the-art systems. | Dedicated benchmarks with multi-paragraph noisy contexts are needed to disentangle factuality from faithfulness in RAG evaluation. | Larger model size does not reliably translate into improved faithfulness under unreliable retrieved evidence.
rationale: FaithEval is an ICLR 2025 benchmark specifically designed to test LLM faithfulness under three classes of unreliable evidence (unanswerable, inconsistent, counterfactual) that directly mirror real-world RAG retrieval failures. With 4.9K validated samples across 10 source datasets and evaluation of 18 proprietary/open models, plus analyses of CoT, decoding strategies, and sycophancy from task-specific instructions, it provides a venue-backbone evaluation reference for a robust-RAG survey. It belongs in the evaluation section as a primary benchmark for contextual faithfulness under noisy/conflicting/missing evidence.
caveat: Focused on QA-style multi-paragraph text contexts; does not cover multimodal, agentic, or adversarial poisoning attacks, and counterfactual contexts are synthetic which may bias difficulty.

title: SmartRAG: Jointly Learn RAG-Related Tasks From the Environment Feedback
supports_claims: Joint RL-based optimization of when-to-retrieve, query rewriting, and answer generation outperforms separately trained RAG modules. | Reward shaping with retrieval cost penalties enables adaptive retrieval that avoids unhelpful or unreliable database queries. | Policy networks can learn to abstain from retrieval when the knowledge base lacks relevant evidence, improving cost-quality tradeoffs.
rationale: SmartRAG unifies decision-making, query rewriting, and answer generation into a single policy network trained with PPO using environment feedback rather than proxy supervision. It directly addresses action-control aspects of robust RAG by learning when retrieval is beneficial vs. when the model or retriever cannot provide useful evidence, which is central to handling unreliable evidence. Empirical analysis on OpenBookQA/MedQA-cn/ARC-c shows the model learns to skip retrieval when the database is uninformative, a key robustness behavior. Placement under main:control is appropriate as the contribution is primarily about adaptive retrieval policy learning.
caveat: Focuses on open-domain QA with Bing search and does not explicitly study adversarial or poisoned evidence; robustness to unreliable evidence is implicit rather than measured.
notes: ICLR 2025 paper; code promised upon acceptance.

title: NeuroGenPoisoning: Neuron-Guided Attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Generation of LLM via Genetic Optimization of External Knowledge
supports_claims: Neuron-level attribution can guide scalable poisoning of RAG external knowledge, exposing a new attack surface beyond surface-level prompt manipulation. | Knowledge conflict between parametric memory and retrieved evidence is exploitable via targeted activation of context-sensitive neurons, with attack success exceeding 90% across multiple LLMs and QA datasets. | Existing RAG poisoning defenses must consider internal representation dynamics, not just retrieval-level filtering, to address sophisticated genetic-optimization attacks.
rationale: This NeurIPS 2025 paper introduces NeuroGenPoisoning, an attack framework that combines neuron attribution (via Integrated Gradients) with genetic optimization to craft adversarial external knowledge that overrides LLM parametric memory in RAG settings. It directly addresses the unreliable-evidence threat model central to robust RAG by demonstrating scalable poisoning under knowledge conflict, with rigorous comparison to PoisonedRAG and explicit mechanistic analysis of poison-responsive neurons. Belongs in the security/integrity section as a key attack baseline informing the survey's discussion of RAG vulnerabilities and defense requirements. Risk of overclaim is minor since results are empirical on open-source LLMs and white-box attribution access is assumed.
caveat: Requires white-box attribution access (intermediate neuron activations), limiting realistic threat scope; black-box extension is future work.
notes: Cite alongside PoisonedRAG, BadRAG, and Pandora as part of the RAG poisoning attack lineage; useful for discussing how knowledge conflict resolution at neuron level can be weaponized.

title: Training Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Question Answering through Backtracking Correction
